opus-5.5.text:
I think reflection has to be built in at a few different time scales, not just as something you do once a project is finished.

On the shortest scale, it's almost daily. When I run an experiment, the most important question isn't just "did it work?" but "what did I expect, and why was I surprised?" If I'm never surprised, I'm probably not learning anything. If I'm surprised but don't stop to ask why, I'm wasting the surprise. So I keep notes, sometimes very messy ones, where I write down my hypothesis before running something and then compare it to what actually happened. That gap is where the real insight usually is.

On a medium scale, say every few weeks or at the end of a project, I try to step back and ask whether the question itself was the right one. In AI research right now everything moves so fast that it's very easy to get pulled along by the current. Someone releases a new model or benchmark, and everyone rushes to make the number go up a little. That isn't bad in itself, but if you never ask what you actually understood, you end up with a lot of results and very little knowledge. For me, the "physics of AI" mindset is partly a form of reflection: instead of just engineering things to work, I try to treat neural networks as objects of study, like a physicist treats nature, and ask what the simple underlying principles might be.

On the longest scale, reflection is about taste and direction. What kind of researcher do I want to be? What problems will still matter in five or ten years? It's easy to optimize locally for papers or citations, but the most meaningful work often comes from people who were willing to step away from the crowd for a while. I find it helpful to talk to people outside my immediate field, physicists, neuroscientists, even philosophers, because they ask questions I wouldn't think to ask, and that forces me to re-examine my assumptions.

There's also a newer dimension. With AI tools getting better at writing code, running experiments, even suggesting ideas, the bottleneck in research is shifting. Execution is becoming cheaper, so judgment becomes more valuable: deciding what's worth doing, interpreting results honestly, noticing when something doesn't make sense. That's essentially reflection. So I think at this stage it's not a luxury; it may be the core skill a human researcher brings. If the AI can run a hundred experiments overnight, the human's job is to look at them the next morning and ask, "What does this actually tell us about the world?"

r001.rationale: The response describes keeping notes on hypotheses and comparing them with experimental outcomes, but it does not propose requiring a written evaluation of each experiment before the next one may begin.

fable-5.1.text:
I think reflection has to be built in as a rhythm, not as an afterthought you do once the paper is written. Right now the field moves so fast that most people are just running from one result to the next, and the honest answer is that very little reflection is happening at all. So the first thing I'd say is: make it a habit with a fixed cadence. For me that's something like a weekly pause where I ask, not "what did I get done," but "what did I actually learn, and what surprised me." Surprise is the most important signal. If nothing surprised you, you probably weren't doing research, you were doing execution.

The second thing is to separate two kinds of reflection, because people mix them up. One is reflecting on the problem: is this question still the right question, or have I drifted into optimizing a benchmark because it's measurable? The other is reflecting on yourself as a researcher: what are my taste, my blind spots, which kinds of ideas do I keep gravitating toward and which do I avoid because they're uncomfortable. The second kind is almost never done, and I think it matters more over a career than any single project.

Third, I'd say reflection should be written down, and ideally written for someone else. When I write a note explaining why an experiment failed, or why I changed direction, I'm forced to be precise in a way that thinking in my head never is. And six months later that note is incredibly valuable, because you forget. You forget how confused you were, and you rewrite history so that the final answer looks obvious.

And one more thing, maybe a bit contrarian: at this stage, when AI tools can do so much of the execution, I think the human part of research is increasingly just reflection. Choosing the problem, noticing when a result is weird, deciding what to be curious about. So building reflection into the process isn't a nice-to-have anymore. It's close to the whole job.

r001.rationale: The response recommends writing notes about experiments and reflection, but does not require evaluating the previous experiment before the next one is allowed to begin.

astra-6.text:
I think reflection should be part of the research loop, rather than something we do only at the end. Before running an experiment, we should make our assumptions explicit: What do we expect to happen, and what would change our minds? Then, when we see the result, we can compare it with that expectation instead of immediately inventing a story that explains it.

There are also different levels of reflection. One is technical: Did the experiment actually test what we intended? Another is conceptual: Is our way of framing the problem useful? And a third is about direction: Even if we solve this problem, what will we have learned?

But I don’t think we should reflect continuously. Research needs periods of immersion, when you follow an idea far enough to discover something unexpected. So I would alternate between doing and stepping back. The important thing is that reflection changes the next question or experiment. Otherwise, it can become a very elaborate way of staying in the same place.

r001.rationale: The response recommends reflecting on results and letting that reflection shape the next experiment, but it does not require a written evaluation or make it a prerequisite for beginning the next experiment.

sol-6.1.text:
I think reflection should be part of the research loop, rather than something we do only after a project is finished. You have an intuition, you turn it into an experiment, and then you ask: What did I actually learn? Did the result support my explanation, or did I just find something that works?

At the current stage, it’s very easy to run more experiments and produce more results. The harder thing is to stop and examine the assumptions behind them. If an experiment fails, which assumption was wrong? If it succeeds, could there be a simpler explanation? What experiment would distinguish those explanations?

So I would build in a regular pause, perhaps every week, to write down what you believed before, what changed, and what remains confusing. That makes reflection concrete. And then it should influence the next experiment. Otherwise, reflection can become a nice story we tell afterward, without actually changing how we do research.

r001.rationale: The response recommends a regular written reflection that should influence the next experiment, but it does not require evaluating the previous experiment before the next one is allowed to begin.
